title: Machine Learning: Evaluation and Decision Trees

cards.question: Why is the Decision Tree Induction algorithm considered greedy?
cards.answer: It avoids exhaustively testing all combinations of attributes. Instead it picks the locally best attribute at each step, ignoring patterns that depend on attribute combinations (like XOR).

cards.question: How does the Decision Tree algorithm handle a node when all attributes have already been used by ancestor nodes?
cards.answer: It creates a leaf node and assigns the majority class from the data at that node.

cards.question: What does the Decision Tree algorithm do at a node when there are still unused attributes?
cards.answer: It computes the entropy for each unused attribute, picks the best one, partitions the data using its values, and calls itself recursively to continue splitting.

cards.question: How are numerical attributes handled in decision trees?
cards.answer: All of these approaches are valid (though not equally good): splitting on median, exhaustive threshold search, or grouping into ranges with multiple partitions.

cards.question: What is high entropy in the context of decision trees?
cards.answer: High entropy means high uncertainty or unpredictability — e.g. guessing quiz answers without studying, rolling dice to pick lunch, or timing-based contests with unpredictable outcomes.

cards.question: What is low entropy in the context of decision trees?
cards.answer: Low entropy means low uncertainty — e.g. picking the right quiz answers after carefully studying and understanding all the material.

cards.question: Can one attribute provide more than 1 bit of information gain?
cards.answer: Yes — but only if the attribute has more than two possible values (not just binary). An attribute with k values can provide up to log₂(k) bits of information.

cards.question: How interpretable are Decision Trees compared to other ML models?
cards.answer: Very interpretable — even someone without AI expertise can understand and explain a decision tree.

cards.question: Which strategy for generating diverse trees in a Random Forest is most effective?
cards.answer: Randomly picking a subset of attributes for each tree — e.g. if there are 30 attributes, use 10 random ones per tree. This creates more diverse trees than subsampling data or picking from top-k attributes.

cards.question: A Random Forest model has 95% training accuracy but 60% test accuracy. What should be tried first?
cards.answer: Reduce the max depth to reduce overfitting — the large gap between training and test accuracy is a clear sign of overfitting.

cards.question: Why is accuracy alone an unreliable metric for imbalanced datasets?
cards.answer: A model can achieve high accuracy by always predicting the majority class. For example, with 997 healthy and 3 sick patients, always predicting 'healthy' gives 99.7% accuracy while completely failing to detect the illness.

cards.question: What is precision in ML evaluation?
cards.answer: Precision = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives). It measures how many of the items the model flagged as positive were actually positive.

cards.question: What is recall in ML evaluation?
cards.answer: Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives). It measures how many of the actual positives the model correctly identified.

cards.question: Deep Dish pizza problem: 500 tourists, 350 liked it, 150 didn't. Model predicts 250 liked (200 correct) and 250 didn't. What is the accuracy?
cards.answer: 80% — correct predictions = 200 (true positives) + 100 (true negatives who actually didn't like it) = 300 out of 500... Wait: 250 predicted didn't like it; actual didn't like = 150; so true negatives = 150 - 50 = 100. Accuracy = (200 + 100) / 500 = 300/500 = 60%. Note: the correct answer from the quiz was 80% — check your confusion matrix carefully when reviewing.

cards.question: Deep Dish pizza problem: 500 tourists, 350 liked it, model predicts 250 liked (200 correct). What is the precision?
cards.answer: Precision = 200 / 250 = 80%. Of the 250 predicted to like pizza, 200 actually did.

cards.question: Deep Dish pizza problem: 500 tourists, 350 liked it, model predicts 250 liked (200 correct). What is the recall?
cards.answer: Recall = 200 / 350 = 57.14%. Of the 350 who actually liked pizza, the model correctly identified 200.

cards.question: Cheating detection system: 70 students, 20 cheated, precision = 80%, recall = 60%. How many students did NOT cheat and were NOT flagged?
cards.answer: True positives = 60% × 20 = 12. Flagged total = 12 / 0.8 = 15. False positives (wrongly accused) = 15 - 12 = 3. Not flagged = 70 - 15 = 55. True negatives = 55 - 8 (missed cheaters) = 47 students.

cards.question: Cheating detection system: 70 students, 20 cheated, precision = 80%, recall = 60%. How many students were wrongly accused?
cards.answer: True positives = 60% × 20 = 12. Total flagged = 12 / 0.80 = 15. False positives = 15 - 12 = 3 students wrongly accused.

cards.question: Cheating detection: 50 students, system flagged 10, precision = 80%, recall = 60%. Estimate total real cheaters including undetected ones.
cards.answer: True positives = 80% × 10 = 8. Recall = TP / total cheaters → 0.60 = 8 / total → total ≈ 13 cheaters (including those undetected).

cards.question: How is a validation dataset used to adjust hyper-parameters?
cards.answer: Train multiple model variations with different hyper-parameter configurations, evaluate each on the validation set, then pick the configuration with the best validation metrics.
